summary:
Pskov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment updated 11 June 2025) sets out as the baseline for this region. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. The note records no findings specific to Pskov Oblast or to the Northwestern Federal District.

Penalties under that baseline are severe. The 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. The 2023 Supreme Court designation of the International LGBT Movement as an extremist organisation carries 2 to 6 years for participating and 6 to 10 years for organising.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that explicitly justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, two of whom were sentenced to prison and one of whom died by suicide in pretrial detention; separately, 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, with participants facing up to 12 years in prison.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and carry out manual labour before escaping.
tangentialFactors:
Official warning levels directed at LGBT travellers are unusually explicit. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers, while the UK Home Office note advises against all but essential travel.

Enforcement has expanded in volume as well as in severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases brought under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes yielded more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) for the state budget across two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues were raided the same night. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia under the designation. No source in the inventory records any enforcement measure, raid or prosecution located in Pskov Oblast itself, and no comparison point from an adjacent region is available; the only sub-national illustrations available are from other parts of the country.
localsOnly:
Residents of Pskov Oblast share the national legal position with no regional carve-out. There is no route to legal gender recognition, no access to gender-affirming care after the 2023 prohibition, no same-sex marriage or partner recognition, and no anti-discrimination protection specific to gender identity or sexual orientation.

Residents risk both administrative and criminal records. Displaying a banned symbol is prosecuted under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses, while participation in the designated extremist organisation is prosecuted criminally; between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people nationwide were caught in convictions, detentions and extremism proceedings.

Protection machinery exists but operates abroad. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard against which UK asylum claims from Russian nationals are assessed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement data specific to Pskov Oblast was located in the inventory: whether any of the 101 extremism convictions or the 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 were recorded in this oblast is not stated by the sources and remains unresolved.

The UK Home Office note contains no Northwestern Federal District-specific findings, so any divergence between this region and the national baseline is unresolved rather than confirmed as absent.

The documented deprivation-of-liberty and forced-treatment case concerns a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, not Pskov Oblast; no comparable reporting about facilities operating in this oblast was sourced.

Entry screening practice at regional border and airport points, and any regional ministry guidance on document inspection for transgender travellers, is not covered by the inventory and is unresolved.
